meta.title: Unit 1 Lab, Checkpoint 1: Density and Measurement

modules.intro: Measure all four required samples at the bench. Record every reading in your physical notebook as you take it, then transcribe it here. Pick the volume technique that fits each sample's geometry, and hold the precision your instruments actually give you.
modules.title: Measurement

blocks.content:
**Record your set letter with every sample number.** Sample sets are not identical. Different sets use different form factors, so the volume technique that fits sample B-2 may not fit sample C-2, and your neighbor's numbers are not a check on yours.

**Work in grams and centimeters.** Published density is reported in g/cm3, so a mass in kilograms or a volume in mm3 will throw your comparison off by a factor of 1000 in the next module.

For each sample:

1. Identify the shape and decide whether a volume formula fits it or whether it needs fluid displacement.
2. Take the measurements that technique requires. Repeat each one. If two readings disagree, re-seat the instrument and take a third.
3. Weigh the sample on the precision scale.
4. Record everything in your notebook first, with the sample number, then transcribe it into the table below.

Samples 5 and 6 are bonus. They are worth no points here. Attempt them only after all four required samples are complete.

columns.tip: The set letter and the sample number, for example B-3. Both, every row.
columns.label: Set / Sample #

columns.tip: Rectangular bar, round rod, tube, sheet, irregular.
columns.label: Shape

columns.tip: Dimensional or Displacement. Say which one you used and why it fits this sample.
columns.label: Volume technique

columns.tip: Every dimension the formula needs, with units, at full caliper resolution. For displacement, the starting and ending fluid levels.
columns.label: Measurements taken

columns.tip: Calculated or displaced. 1 mL displaced = 1 cm3 exactly.
columns.label: Volume (cm3)

columns.tip: From the precision scale, in grams.
columns.label: Mass (g)

columns.label: Notebook page

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: All four required samples have a recorded shape, a named volume technique, every measurement that technique needs, a volume in cm3, and a mass in grams.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: All four required samples are measured, with one sample missing its shape, its named technique, or one required dimension.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Two or three samples are completely measured, or all four are present with volume or mass missing on more than one.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than two samples are measured, or no measurements are recorded.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: Every dimension and mass is recorded to the full resolution the instrument reads, trailing zeros are retained where they are significant, and the calculated volume carries the same precision as its inputs, on all four samples.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Recorded to instrument resolution on all four samples, with precision dropped or digits added beyond the instrument's reading on one or two individual values.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Recorded to instrument resolution on two or three samples, or resolution is correct throughout but values are rounded to different precision from one sample to the next.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Values are recorded without regard to instrument resolution, or fewer than two samples carry usable precision.

modules.intro: Calculate density from your own measurements, compare each result against a published value you look up yourself, and state a first identification for every required sample based on that comparison.
modules.title: Density, Comparison, and Hypothesis

blocks.content:
Density is mass divided by volume, in g/cm3.

Published property values come from **MatWeb**. OnlineMetals, Industrial Metal Supply, and McMaster-Carr are price and availability sources, not property databases, and some carry no property data for plastics at all. Whichever source you use, name it.

`percent error = |measured - published| / published x 100`

A percent error in the thousands is a units problem, not a discovery. Check grams and cm3 before you check anything else.

The most accurate results in the class earn IDEA Coins.

columns.tip: The set letter and the sample number, for example B-3. Both, every row.
columns.label: Set / Sample #

columns.tip: Show the division with your actual numbers, for example 51.3 g / 6.44 cm3.
columns.label: Density calculation

columns.tip: Your result, rounded to the precision your measurements support.
columns.label: Measured density (g/cm3)

columns.tip: The value you looked up for the material you think this is.
columns.label: Published density (g/cm3)

columns.tip: Name it. MatWeb, or whichever published source the value came from.
columns.label: Source

columns.tip: Calculated against the published value, written as a number with a percent sign.
columns.label: Percent error

blocks.prompt: State your first identification for each of the four required samples. For each one, give the density you measured and the published density you matched it to. Where two candidate materials sit close enough that density alone cannot separate them, say so and name both.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: Density is computed for all four required samples, each showing the mass and volume values being divided, with the result stated in g/cm3.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: All four are computed with the division shown, with one arithmetic error or one unit stated incorrectly.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Two or three samples are computed with the division shown, or all four appear as results only with no division shown.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than two densities are computed, or no density values are given.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: Each of the four required samples is compared against a published density from a named source, with percent error computed and written as a number.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: All four are compared against a published value, with the source unnamed on one or more samples, or percent error missing on one sample.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than four samples are compared against a published value, or no percent error is computed.

levels.label: Complete
levels.descriptor: An identification is named for each of the four required samples, and each names both the measured density and the published density it was matched to.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: An identification is named for all four samples, with the supporting density values missing on one or more of them.

levels.label: Absent
levels.descriptor: Fewer than four samples are identified, or identifications are given with no reference to density.
